did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm opens with the title “For Solomon” and a prayer that God would grant the king justice and righteousness so that he could rule fairly.
Did you know? In the opening verses, the king’s central role is to judge fairly and especially to protect the poor and vulnerable among the people.
Did you know? According to the psalm, worthy rule is measured not only by political power but also by the ability to rescue the needy and crush the oppressor.
Did you know? The king’s success is compared to rain falling on grass that has been mown and to showers that water the earth. The image conveys a life-giving, gentle, and beneficial influence.
Did you know? The flourishing of the righteous and “abundant peace” are presented together, as though social justice and peace were two sides of good governance.
Did you know? The description of the king’s kingdom as extending “from sea to sea” and to the ends of the earth presents a realm of worldwide scope, expressed in broad poetic language.
Did you know? The psalm mentions kings from distant lands—Tarshish, the islands, Sheba, and Seba—bringing tribute and gifts to the king.
Did you know? Verses 12–14 repeatedly emphasize rescuing the needy, the poor, and the helpless; human dignity and the saving of their lives are at the center of the description of the ideal king.

Did you know? The king’s name is described as enduring forever and as a source of blessing: “May all nations be blessed through him.” Thus, the king is presented not only as a ruler but also as a symbol of blessing.

Did you know? The final verse states: “The prayers of David son of Jesse are ended.” This verse concludes the collection of David’s prayers in the psalm and appears at the end of the second book of Psalms.
